hops.title: Compare it: a pelican's pouch and a kitchen colander
hops.text: Hold up a colander before the buffet. A brown pelican can scoop up fish and as much as three gallons of water in the stretchy pouch under its bill. Water slips out at the corners of its mouth. Like a colander, the bill lets the water go and keeps the food. Then the bird swallows the fish.

sources.citation: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, "Brown pelican"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A brown pelican floating on blue water with water running from the corner of its mouth above its large throat pouch.
image.caption: A brown pelican lets water slip out the corners of its mouth and keeps the fish, like a colander.

hops.title: Point at it: a robin tilting its head on the grass
hops.text: On a walk, with you close by, watch for an American robin hopping across a lawn or park grass. See how it stops and tilts its head sideways? A robin's eyes sit on the sides of its head. Tilting helps it get a close look at one spot on the ground. Robins can also use sound to find worms.

sources.citation: Washington State University, Ask Dr. Universe, "How do robins find worms?"
Montana State University Library, Acoustic Atlas, "Can robins hear worms?"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A grown-up and child seen from behind watching an American robin tilt its head on a grassy lawn.
image.caption: A robin tilts its head to get a close look at one spot of grass while it hunts for worms.

hops.title: Say it: a beak is covered in fingernail stuff
hops.text: "Tap your fingernail. A bird's beak is covered in the same kind of stuff, called keratin. It wears down and grows back a little, yet one bird does not reshape its beak into a spoon." Use this line when your child asks if a bird can just grow a new beak for new food.

sources.citation: Illinois Department of Natural Resources, Kids for Conservation (January 2019)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A child's hand tapping a fingernail near a window where a northern cardinal perches on a branch.
image.caption: A bird's beak is covered in keratin, the same kind of stuff as fingernails, which wears down and grows back.
